items.t: A cavity wall is two walls, called leaves, with a gap between them called the cavity. The outer leaf is brick and the inner leaf is block. Wall ties hold the two leaves together. This is a short length of a longer wall, part-built.

Below ground is the substructure. The damp-proof course (DPC) is a waterproof strip laid in a bed joint (horizontal mortar joint) of both leaves. It goes at least 150 mm above the outside ground, so damp from the ground can’t rise up the wall.

The inner leaf (blockwork) goes up first. It is called the leading leaf. A concrete lintel spans the window opening. On site the leaves go up in lifts, a bit at a time — here each one is shown going up in one go so it’s easy to see.

Wall ties join the two leaves. In the main wall they go no more than 900 mm apart across and 450 mm apart up, staggered. Beside an opening they go within 225 mm of the edge, no more than 300 mm apart up. They are bedded in mortar as each lift is built, and kept off the DPC.

Partial-fill insulation boards are fixed tight against the inner leaf. Retaining clips on the wall ties hold them in place. At least 50 mm of clear cavity is left between the boards and the outer leaf.

The outer leaf (facing brickwork) goes up. Each tie sits at least 50 mm into each leaf, level or falling slightly outwards, with its drip in the middle of the clear cavity, pointing down. Keep mortar out of the cavity.

At the window, cavity closers close the cavity at the reveals (the sides of the opening). Above the lintel, a cavity tray with stop ends catches water in the cavity and runs it outwards. Weep holes let it out — at least two per opening, no more than 450 mm apart.

Here the wall is cut through. Rain that soaks through the outer leaf runs down its inside face. It drips off the tie drips and drains away below the DPC — the cavity carries on at least 225 mm below it. Above the window, the tray and weep holes send it outside. The inner leaf stays dry.

Mortar droppings on ties or at the bottom of the cavity, ties sloping inwards, or a loose insulation board all make a bridge. Water crosses the cavity and causes damp inside. Now try the Spot the faults challenge.

quiz.q: In the main wall, what is the maximum spacing for wall ties?
Which way should the drip on a wall tie point?
o: Down, in the middle of the clear cavity

quiz.q: How high above the outside ground should the DPC be?
Where do partial-fill insulation boards go?
o: In the middle of the cavity
Against the inner leaf, keeping at least 50 mm clear cavity

quiz.q: What is the job of a weep hole above a cavity tray?
o: To let water drain out of the cavity
To let you check the wall ties
To let air dry the bricks
To drain water off the DPC at ground level

items.t: This is the disc brake from one wheel of a car, with the brake pedal and master cylinder. Some parts are cut in half so you can see inside. Drag to turn it. Pinch or scroll to zoom.
When you press the brake pedal, it pushes a rod into the master cylinder. The pedal works like a lever, so a small push from your foot becomes a big push.

The master cylinder pushes brake fluid (orange) along the pipe. A liquid cannot be squashed, so the push at the pedal comes out just as strong at the wheel. The arrows show the pressure travelling to the caliper.
The fluid pushes the caliper piston out. The piston pushes the inner pad onto the disc. The caliper then slides on its pins and pulls the outer pad onto the other side.
The pads rub on the spinning disc. This friction slows the wheel. The movement of the car turns into heat. Hard braking from high speed can make the disc glow red hot.
When you let go, the fluid pressure drops. The rubber piston seal pulls the piston back a little, so the pads stop touching the disc and the wheel can turn freely.
These pads are worn thin. The piston has to come out further, so the pedal goes down further. Thin pads grip less, so the car takes longer to stop. Listen for the squeal of the wear indicator.

items.h: Fault: air in the brake line
items.t: There is air (white bubbles) in the brake fluid. Air can be squashed, so the pedal feels spongy and sinks towards the floor. The brakes are much weaker. The fix is to bleed the brakes at the bleed nipple.
The brake is now taken apart. Tap or click any part to see what it does and what to check. Look at the pads, the disc, the slide pins and the piston seal.
Step one. Your foot pushes the brake pedal. The pedal pushes a rod into the master cylinder.
Step two. The master cylinder pushes brake fluid along the pipe. Fluid cannot be squashed, so it carries the push to the wheel.
Step three. The fluid pushes the caliper piston out. The piston pushes the inner pad onto the disc, and the caliper slides to pull the outer pad on too.
Step four. The pads rub on the spinning disc. Friction slows the car, and the movement turns into heat.
Step five. You let go. The pressure drops, and the piston seal pulls the piston back a little, so the pads let go of the disc.
The driver presses it with their foot. It works like a lever to make the push bigger. What to check: The pedal should feel firm and stop well above the floor.
Turns the push from the pedal into brake fluid pressure. What to check: No fluid leaks around the master cylinder.
Holds spare brake fluid for the system. What to check: Fluid level between MIN and MAX. A low level can mean worn pads or a leak.
Carry the brake fluid from the master cylinder to the caliper. What to check: No leaks, rust or damage. Flexible hoses must not be cracked or bulging.
Holds the piston and pads. It slides on its pins so both pads squeeze the disc. What to check: No fluid leaks. The caliper should slide freely.
Brake fluid pushes it out. It pushes the inner pad onto the disc. What to check: Moves freely. Not seized, rusty or leaking.
A rubber ring. It stops fluid leaking out, and pulls the piston back a little when you let go. What to check: No fluid leaking past the piston.
Let the caliper slide in and out so both pads press evenly. What to check: Slide freely, greased, and rubber boots not split.
Squeeze the disc. The friction between pad and disc slows the wheel. What to check: Enough friction material left (usually at least 3 mm – check the data). No cracks. Even wear.
Turns with the wheel. The pads squeeze it to slow the car. What to check: Smooth surface. No deep scores, cracks or big lip on the edge.
Bolted to the car. Holds the pads and the slide pins. What to check: Bolts tight. Pads slide in it freely.
A small valve used to let air out of the brake fluid. This is called bleeding the brakes. What to check: Not seized, and the dust cap is fitted.

quiz.q: What does the brake pedal push?
o: A rod into the master cylinder

quiz.q: Why is brake fluid used to carry the push to the wheel?
What pushes the brake pads onto the disc?
When the pads squeeze the disc, the car’s movement is turned into…
The pedal feels spongy and sinks nearly to the floor. What is the most likely fault?

items.t: Switch off and unplug the mains cable from the power supply. Work on an antistatic mat, wear an ESD wrist strap connected to ground, and handle parts by their edges.
items.warn: Skipping the wrist strap: a static discharge too small to feel can still damage the CPU or motherboard.

items.t: Use a Torx T20 driver to loosen the three captive force-frame screws in reverse order: 3, then 2, then 1. The numbers are printed on the force frame.
items.warn: Using the wrong bit size can strip the Torx heads. Use a T20.

items.t: The force frame is spring-loaded, so it pops up as the last screw is released. Lift it to the fully open position.
items.warn: Keep fingers, tools and loose items away from the socket area while it is open.

items.t: Pull up the tabs on both sides of the rail frame to release it, then lift it to its upright position. It is spring-loaded too, so keep hold of it.
items.warn: Letting the rail frame snap up or down can knock the socket. Move it gently.

items.t: Slide the clear external cap up and out of the rail frame. Keep it: it goes back in if the board is ever stored or returned without a CPU.
items.warn: The external cap is not the socket cover. The PnP cover cap on the socket stays on for now.

items.h: Slide in the carrier and CPU
items.t: Hold the orange carrier frame by its tab and slide it down the rails until it clicks into place. It only fits one way: the tab faces up and away from the socket.
items.warn: Never take the CPU out of the orange carrier frame, and never force it into the rails.

items.t: Now lift the PnP cover cap off the socket using its tabs. The exposed socket contacts are extremely fragile: don’t touch them or let anything drop onto them.
items.warn: Removing the cap too early leaves the contacts exposed for longer. On this socket the contacts are in the motherboard, so bent contacts usually mean a damaged board.

items.t: Lower the rail frame gently until it latches onto the socket housing, then lower the force frame over it.
items.warn: Never press down on the CPU with your fingers to seat it. The force frame does the clamping.

items.t: Start all three screws in the order 1, 2, 3, then tighten them fully in the same order with a torque-limiting T20 driver. Stop at the click: about 1.6 N·m (14 lbf·in). Check your motherboard manual.
items.warn: Tightening in the wrong order, or over-tightening, can cause serious damage to the socket or the CPU.

items.t: If the cooler has paste pre-applied, don’t add more. Otherwise apply paste as the cooler or paste maker’s guide shows. This large lid needs a pattern that spreads across the whole surface, not one small dot.
items.warn: Too much paste lowers heat conductivity and cooling performance.

items.t: Remove the protective film from the cooler base, lower the cooler straight down onto the CPU, then tighten its screws evenly in a diagonal pattern, a little at a time. Use the cooler’s own instructions and torque, not the socket value.
items.warn: Leaving the protective film on the cooler base blocks heat transfer, so the CPU can overheat.

items.t: Plug the cooler fan into the CPU_FAN header on the motherboard so the board can read its speed and control it. Then reconnect power and check the CPU temperature and fan speed in the BIOS/UEFI.
items.warn: Forgetting to connect the fan, or using the wrong header, means the board can’t properly monitor or control the CPU fan, and the CPU can overheat.

quiz.q: In which order do you loosen the force frame screws?
When do you remove the PnP cover cap from the socket?
o: After the carrier frame and CPU are in the rail frame

quiz.q: On an sTR5 system, where are the fragile contacts (pins)?
o: On the underside of the CPU

quiz.q: How do you tighten the force frame screws?
o: In the order 1 → 2 → 3 until the torque driver clicks (about 1.6 N·m)
As tight as possible with a normal screwdriver

quiz.q: Your new cooler has thermal paste already applied. What do you do?
o: Add a large blob on top for extra cooling
Fit it as supplied without adding more paste
Wipe it off and use one pea-sized dot
Put paste on the motherboard instead

items.t: A CT scanner and a plain X-ray set-up. The patient lies on the table. The doughnut-shaped gantry holds an X-ray tube and a detector array that rotate around the patient. Real equipment is expensive, and X-rays are ionising, so we explore it safely here.

A heated cathode filament releases electrons (thermionic emission). A high voltage accelerates them towards a positive tungsten anode. When they hit it, some of their kinetic energy becomes X-rays and most becomes heat, so the anode spins to spread the heat. Lead collimators shape the beam.

X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by dense bone. This reduction in intensity is attenuation. The detector records how many X-rays arrive: behind bone few arrive, so the image is white; through air-filled lungs many arrive, so it is dark. Try the kV slider.

In CT, the X-ray tube rotates around the patient while the table moves smoothly through the gantry. The detector array opposite measures attenuation along hundreds of lines from every angle. Relative to the patient, the tube traces a spiral (helix), shown in blue. The gantry is shown slowed down.

A computer combines all the measurements to reconstruct cross-sectional images called tomograms, layer by layer. Each pixel gets a CT number in Hounsfield units (HU): air −1000, water 0, fat about −100, soft tissue +30 to +60, bone several hundred or more. Stacked slices build a 3D view. Hover the CT slice to read values.

X-rays are ionising: they can damage healthy cells and slightly increase cancer risk. Under IR(ME)R every exposure must be justified and doses kept as low as reasonably practicable. A chest CT (about 6.6 mSv) is roughly 470 times a chest X-ray (0.014 mSv). Staff use distance, lead shielding and dosemeters. Open the Dose tab.
Doughnut-shaped housing. Inside, the X-ray tube and detectors rotate around the patient. (Front cover cut away here.)
Produces the X-ray beam. It rotates around the patient so attenuation is measured from many angles.
Measures how many X-rays get through the body along each line. Brighter = more X-rays arriving (less attenuation).
Carbon-fibre style top that X-rays pass through easily. In CT it moves the patient smoothly through the gantry.
Chest–abdomen model. The skin and fat layer is see-through so you can watch the beam inside.
Mostly air, so they attenuate X-rays very little and look dark on images. Typical CT number: about −700 HU.
Muscle and blood – similar attenuation to other soft tissue. Typical CT number: about +40 HU.
Solid soft-tissue organ. Typical CT number: about +60 HU.
Air attenuates almost nothing, so it looks black. Typical CT number: about −1000 HU.
Soft-tissue organs near the back. Typical CT number: about +30 HU.
Dense bone with calcium – strongly attenuates X-rays, so it looks white. Typical CT number: about +400 to +1000 HU.
Bone – appears white on X-ray images and CT slices. Typical CT number: about +700 HU.
Breastbone – bone, so it appears white. Typical CT number: about +500 HU.
The cross-section being measured right now. The computer reconstructs it as a tomogram.
Makes X-rays for a plain X-ray image. Its housing is shown see-through.
Heated filament (negative). Electrons escape by thermionic emission.
Positive target. Electrons hit it and some of their kinetic energy becomes X-rays; most becomes heat, so it spins to spread the heat.
Lead shutters that shape the beam so only the area being imaged is exposed.
Records how many X-rays arrive at each point. The image builds up here (older systems used photographic film).
Each slice (tomogram) is stacked in order to build a 3D view of the body.
Stays out of the beam, behind shielding, and wears a personal dosemeter badge (yellow).
Lead absorbs scattered X-rays. In CT, staff normally operate the scanner from a shielded control room.

quiz.q: Match the image to the tissue: on the CT slice in the simulation, which tissue is at each of points A, B, C and D? (Each answer is used once.)
How does an X-ray tube produce X-rays?
o: Electrons from a heated cathode are accelerated into a tungsten anode
A radioactive source inside the tube decays
Light from the filament is filtered into X-rays
The spinning anode creates a magnetic field that emits X-rays

quiz.q: On a projection X-ray image, why does the spine appear white?
o: Bone reflects X-rays back towards the tube
Bone attenuates (absorbs) more X-rays, so fewer reach the detector
Bone gives out its own X-rays
The detector is more sensitive behind bone

quiz.q: How does a CT scanner build up a cross-sectional image?
o: It takes one X-ray photo and cuts it into strips
Detectors measure radiation given out by the patient’s organs
It measures attenuation from many angles as the tube rotates, then a computer reconstructs the slice
It uses sound echoes from the rotating gantry

quiz.q: A region on a CT slice reads −700 HU. Which tissue is it most likely to be?
Using UKHSA typical doses, a chest CT (6.6 mSv) is roughly how many times a chest X-ray (0.014 mSv)?
A radiographer moves from 1 m to 2 m from the source of scatter. What happens to the scatter dose rate?

items.t: In X-ray and CT, radiation passes through the body from a machine. Nuclear medicine works the other way round: a small amount of radioactive tracer goes inside the patient, and a gamma camera or PET scanner detects the gamma rays coming out. The scans show how organs are working, not just their shape.

For a bone scan, technetium-99m (Tc-99m) is attached to a chemical that bone takes up, then injected into an arm vein. Tc-99m gives out only gamma rays (140 keV), which leave the body easily, and has a half-life of about 6 hours. Over 2–3 hours the tracer collects in the bones; the kidneys pass some into the bladder. The syringe is shielded to protect staff.

Gamma rays leave the body in all directions. The lead collimator only lets through gamma rays travelling straight towards the camera; the rest are stopped (red). Each one that gets through makes a flash of light in the sodium iodide crystal. Photomultiplier tubes turn the flash into an electrical pulse, and the computer works out where it happened. The image builds up count by count as the camera sweeps along the body.

Areas that take up more tracer show as darker “hot spots”. Here there is a hot spot in a rib and one in a vertebra. A hot spot means increased bone activity – it could be a healing fracture, infection, arthritis or cancer spread, so doctors use other tests too. Watch the image when the collimator is removed: gamma rays arrive from every angle and the picture blurs.

PET uses a positron-emitting tracer, usually fluorine-18 in FDG, a glucose-like sugar (half-life 110 minutes). Each positron travels less than a millimetre, meets an electron and annihilates, making two 511 keV gamma rays that travel in opposite directions. The ring records pairs arriving at the same moment (coincidence) and the computer builds a 3D image. Combined with CT, it shows active cancer and recurrent tumours.

Activity falls as the tracer decays and is passed out in urine. After one half-life (6 hours) half the Tc-99m is left; after 24 hours about one-sixteenth. A bone scan gives about 4 mSv; PET-CT about 5–18 mSv. Staff use syringe shields, distance, short handling times and personal dosemeters. Patients drink plenty and avoid long close contact with young children and pregnant women for the rest of the day.
Moves the patient under the gamma camera, or through the PET-CT scanner.
See-through so you can watch the tracer and gamma rays inside.
Take up little tracer on a bone scan. In the PET scan, the bright spot in the right lung is a tumour using lots of glucose.
Heart muscle uses a lot of glucose, so it often shows on PET (normal).
Filter tracer out of the blood into urine, so they show faintly.
Collects tracer passed out in urine – it shows strongly on both scans. Emptying it often lowers the dose.
Bone takes up the tracer. The vertebra marked “hot spot” has much more uptake than the others.
Bone takes up the tracer. One rib has a hot spot – increased bone activity.
Bone – takes up the tracer evenly here (normal).
The tracer is injected into an arm vein. A lead or tungsten syringe shield cuts the dose to the hands of the person injecting.
Detects gamma rays coming out of the patient. It gives out no radiation itself. Its cover is see-through here.
Thick lead plate full of narrow holes. Only gamma rays travelling straight along the holes get through, so each count can be traced back to where it came from.
Scintillator: each gamma ray that hits it makes a tiny flash of light.
Turn each faint flash of light into an electrical pulse. The computer compares the pulses to work out where the flash happened.
Adds up the counts to build the image. Areas with more counts have taken up more tracer.
Rings of detectors around the patient. Two detectors flashing at the same moment mean an annihilation happened somewhere on the line between them.
Contains the detector rings. Front cover cut away.
Takes a CT scan in the same visit, so the PET hot spots can be placed exactly on the anatomy.
Keeps handling time short, uses distance and shielding, wears gloves and a personal dosemeter (yellow badge).

quiz.q: In gamma imaging, where does the radiation that makes the image come from?
o: The gamma camera fires it through the patient
A radioactive tracer inside the patient
An X-ray tube under the table

quiz.q: Why is technetium-99m a good tracer for a gamma camera?
o: It gives out alpha particles, which are easy to detect
It gives out only gamma rays (140 keV) and has a half-life of about 6 hours
Its half-life is several years, so it lasts

quiz.q: What does the lead collimator do?
o: Only lets through gamma rays travelling straight towards the camera, so the image is sharp
Protects the patient from radiation given out by the camera

quiz.q: A bone scan shows a hot spot in a rib. What does it tell the doctor?
o: Increased bone activity there – it could be a fracture, infection, arthritis or cancer, so more tests are needed
The rib has no blood supply

quiz.q: What does a PET scanner actually detect?
o: Pairs of 511 keV gamma rays travelling in opposite directions at the same time

quiz.q: A dose of technetium-99m has an activity of 400 MBq at 9 am. Ignoring removal by the body, what is its activity at about 9 pm?
